messages.subject: Re: Question
parts:
Thank you very much Richard. I would try your approach.

Regarding to the original question, for example, it was found that psi correlate with forest percentage, so you have,

              psi      EE
Site 1     0.48     0.053
Site 2     0.76     0.12


Site n    0.32      0.02

You average all the sites and report an overall psi for the study area, not just for the "sample".  Is that correct?  How is the calculation of the overall EE? Should they use the delta method?  I saw this in Linkie 2007 and Karanth 2009.

Best,

Manuel




2012/2/22 Richard Chandler <rcha...@usgs.gov>
Hi Manuel,

This would be a good question for the list as I'm sure other people have the same question. Anyhow, the approach you mention is fine, but if you only want to make know what proportion of the sites *in the sample* were occupied, it would be better to use the new ranef() function. Something like:

re <- ranef(fm)
mean(bup(re, stat="mode"))
colMeans(confint(re))

Richard

I have an specific question.   When doing occupancy models and using covariates I have seen people take an average of the occupancy on all the sites to give an unique value of psi.  Is that correct?  How do you get a EE for that approach?  Is it an alternative to take the average of the covariate and plug-in that value in the formula of the best model?

messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Question
parts:
Hi Manuel,

If you there are covariates of psi, then to make inferences to the entire study area, you need to know the covariate values at each location in the study area. You would then predict psi at each point in the study area and take an average of that. You could use the delta method or bootstrap methods to compute confidence intervals.

Richard
